root.meaning: one who shares bread with you
root.note: cum, ‘with’, + pānis, ‘bread’. First found in the Lex Salica. The TLFi explains it as a translation of a Germanic word such as Gothic gahlaiba.

history: Un copain is someone you share bread with. Late Latin companio is cum, ‘with’, plus panis, ‘bread’. It first turns up in the Lex Salica, the law of the Franks, and the TLFi explains it as a Latin translation of a Germanic soldiers' word: Gothic gahlaiba, ‘one who shares bread’, from hlaib, ‘loaf’. Old French had two forms of one noun: cumpainz for the subject and cumpaignun for the object, both in the Song of Roland. The object form became compagnon. The subject form, compain, lost its nasal sound and became copain, recorded with the sense ‘friend, mate’ in 1838. So compagnon and copain are one word in two grammatical cases. Today mon copain can also mean ‘my boyfriend’, and ma copine ‘my girlfriend’.
historyEinfach: Copain comes from Latin companio: cum means ‘with’, and panis means ‘bread’. A companio was someone who eats bread with you. In old French there were two forms: compain and compagnon. Compagnon is still a French word. Compain became copain. Mon copain is ‘my friend’ or ‘my boyfriend’.

elsewhere.text: English companion is the French compagnon, the other half of the same Old French noun. Copain and companion are therefore close relatives.
